column5: F: Where does all this come from? | M: One kernel.
column6: F: Where does all this come from? | M: One kernel, start to finish. A building's schedule becomes a project order. The order buys material, the material is received, issued to the site, invoiced and paid. The dashboard reads those same rows. Twelve test projects here.

column5: F: And this is the dashboard? | M: One screen.
column6: F: And this is the dashboard? | M: One screen. Twelve projects, all active. Planned, about four thousand dollars. Spent so far, about thirteen thousand. The forecast, about twenty-four thousand, carries a warning when spent and done are not measured on one basis. Health: two green, three amber, six red.

column5: F: Which projects make that number? | M: Click it.
column6: F: Which projects make that number? | M: Click it. A panel opens with the twelve projects, each with its planned amount.

column5: F: And what has been spent? | M: Click spent.
column6: F: And what has been spent? | M: Click spent. Twelve rows again, each project's actual cost. It comes from the stock issued to site, completed project issues, not from a typed number.

column5: F: Why does that forecast carry a warning? | M: Spent and done differ.
column6: F: Why does that forecast carry a warning? | M: On this project what has been spent is far above what is done, so they are not on one basis. The forecast is a proposed definition, and here it says so instead of pretending to be a result.

column5: F: What is amber? | M: Click it.
column6: F: What is amber? | M: Click it. Three projects, each listed with the reason: a phase overdue, or spent running ahead of progress.

column5: F: Is there a picture of the portfolio? | M: The map.
column6: F: Is there a picture of the portfolio? | M: Each bubble is a project: days behind across, spent against plan up. Hover shows the numbers, click opens the project.

column5: F: What should I look at first? | M: Needs attention.
column6: F: What should I look at first? | M: Needs attention. Six projects, the worst first, each with its reason in plain words.

column5: F: And the left menu? | M: Projects.
column6: F: And the left menu? | M: Projects lists every project that passes the filters, with planned, actual and committed amounts. The Dashboard item is the glance itself.

column5: F: Money? | M: Budget and cost.
column6: F: Money? | M: Budget and cost shows the money per project: planned, committed, invoiced and actual, in the project's own currency.

column5: F: And buying? | M: Procurement risks, proposed.
column6: F: And buying? | M: Procurement risks, with proposed definitions awaiting the client. Five purchase orders are still open, drafts not yet completed.

column5: F: Anything waiting for me? | M: Approval pending.
column6: F: Anything waiting for me? | M: Approval pending counts the workflow approvals waiting for someone to act. Ten, and the badge on the menu is the same number.

column5: F: And the end of a project? | M: Handover, proposed.
column6: F: And the end of a project? | M: Handover, again proposed definitions. One project is ready to hand over; none has been marked done yet.

column5: F: Can I go inside one project? | M: Click it.
column6: F: Can I go inside one project? | M: Click it. A page of its own, in tabs. Schedule draws four phases and, under them, eight dated tasks. Procurement shows the supply chain order by order: received, invoiced, paid, each document one click from its record.

column5: F: Can I change how it looks? | M: Layout and skin.
column6: F: Can I change how it looks? | M: Classic or Executive, light or dark. Same data underneath: the numbers do not move when the look does. A formula marker on each tile shows how it is calculated, and a table view lists any chart.
